messages.subject: Re: [knitr] How to programatically tell the difference between a knitr and an Sweave Rnw file?
messages.subject_clean: [knitr] How to programatically tell the difference between a knitr and an Sweave Rnw file?
messages.body_plain:
Just a quick follow-up:

1. As I said, knitr is no longer compatible with the Sweave syntax;
one has to make a choice between the two, although there is
Sweave2knitr() to help those who are not on the knitr boat yet:
http://yihui.name/knitr/demo/sweave/

2. R 3.0.0 will allow non-Sweave vignettes:
http://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/r-devel/R-exts.html#Non_002dSweave-vignettes

The current method is to specify the weave engine in meta comments,
e.g. %\VignetteEngine{knitr}. In fact this also applies to R Markdown
vignettes (*.Rmd) which have also become first-class citizens in R
3.0.0. Brave beta testers can check out the latest development version
R from SVN and play with this brand new feature.

Regards,
Yihui
--
Yihui Xie <xiey...@gmail.com>
Phone: 515-294-2465 Web: http://yihui.name
Department of Statistics, Iowa State University
2215 Snedecor Hall, Ames, IA

messages.subject: Need help on the title of the knitr book
messages.subject_clean: Need help on the title of the knitr book
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

As a few of you might have known, I have finished the draft of the
knitr book in the winter. It is expected to come out in the summer.
Now I have got a question about the title of the book: originally I
used "Dynamic Report Generation with R and knitr", and one reviewer
said this was too narrow -- Dynamic Reports should be Dynamic
Documents instead. Although I agree what I'm really talking about is
Dynamic Documents, I doubt if the general readers know what this book
is about by looking at a title like "Dynamic Documents with R and
knitr".

What do you think?

Regards,
Yihui
--
Yihui Xie <xiey...@gmail.com>
Phone: 515-294-2465 Web: http://yihui.name
Department of Statistics, Iowa State University
2215 Snedecor Hall, Ames, IA

messages.subject: Re: [knitr] Need help on the title of the knitr book
messages.subject_clean: [knitr] Need help on the title of the knitr book
messages.body_plain:
I also use the term "dynamic" (reports/documents), but I'm starting to
question it because it is a bit misleading.  To me it hints that the
final document is dynamic/interactive (e.g. HTML+Javascript) and not
that the process of creating it is "dynamic" (which is the main
intention of the word).  Also, in the latter sense "dynamic" and
"generation" are redundant.  Maybe you can find a better title by
dropping the term "dynamic" and instead use terms such as "easy",
"powerful", ...?

My $.02 and best wishes for the book

/Henrik

messages.subject: Re: [knitr] Need help on the title of the knitr book
messages.subject_clean: [knitr] Need help on the title of the knitr book
messages.body_plain:
"dynamic document" sounds good to me.  I think most people use "interactive" when they mean interactive; while dynamic is used more loosely.  Sweave has always been referred to using the word "dynamic".  Temple-Lang and Gentleman refer to "dynamic documents" in this way in doi:10.1198/106186007X178663.

The term "Document" does sound a bit more general than "report", which seems appropriate as knitr generalizes the Sweave concept of a document.  I don't know the literature that well, but it seems that would be consistent with its use elsewhere.  I guess no choice will make all readers happy.  I've never found the magic word to explain the idea; I think knitr is one of those things you have to see to believe.

-Carl

messages.subject: Re: [knitr] MathJax: external link
messages.subject_clean: [knitr] MathJax: external link
messages.body_plain:
Here is a way to use a local fallback option for mathjax.

Download the contents of this directory: https://github.com/ramnathv/slidifyLibraries/tree/master/inst/libraries/widgets/mathjax

And include the following script in your html. It basically uses the CDN to serve mathjax assets when online, but falls back to a stripped down local version if the user is offline.

<!-- MathJax: Fall back to local if CDN offline but local image fonts are not supported (saves >100MB) -->
<script type="text/x-mathjax-config">
  MathJax.Hub.Config({
    tex2jax: {
      inlineMath: [['$','$'], ['\\(','\\)']],
      processEscapes: true
    }
  });
</script>
<script type="text/javascript" src="http://cdn.mathjax.org/mathjax/2.0-latest/MathJax.js?config=TeX-AMS-MML_HTMLorMML"></script>
<!-- <script src="https://c328740.ssl.cf1.rackcdn.com/mathjax/2.0-latest/MathJax.js?config=TeX-AMS-MML_HTMLorMML">
</script> -->
<script>window.MathJax || document.write('<script type="text/x-mathjax-config">MathJax.Hub.Config({"HTML-CSS":{imageFont:null}});<\/script><script src="path/to/mathjax/MathJax.js?config=TeX-AMS-MML_HTMLorMML"><\/script>')
</script>

messages.subject: knitr version 1.1
messages.subject_clean: knitr version 1.1
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I released knitr 1.1 to CRAN a few days ago:
http://cran.r-project.org/package=knitr See all new features and
changes at https://github.com/yihui/knitr/blob/master/NEWS.md#changes-in-knitr-version-11

The version 1.0 does not imply perfect stability or maturity. The
major version number was bumped from 0.x to 1.x due to a number of
important features and the breaking of compatibility with Sweave
(http://yihui.name/knitr/demo/sweave/). A brief summary of recent
features:

1. (please regard this one as "experimental") from R 3.0.0 we will be
able to compile package vignettes with knitr, even including R
Markdown vignettes (http://yihui.name/knitr/demo/vignette/)
2. the encoding argument in knit() allows one to specify the encoding
of the source document, which may benefit international users (this
has also been supported in RStudio, and the next version of LyX will
also support encoding correctly)
3. you can publish blog posts from R to WordPress using R Markdown and
the knit2wp() function
(http://yihui.name/en/2013/02/publishing-from-r-knitr-to-wordpress/)
4. Rcpp is supported in code chunks (see http://gallery.rcpp.org for
an application), and more languages have been added (Perl, Bash,
CoffeeScript, ... http://yihui.name/knitr/demo/engines/)
5. A Shiny notebook was added as a demo (http://glimmer.rstudio.com/yihui/knitr)

I thank the amazing R community; in particular, I thank all
contributors who sent me over 50 pull requests
(https://github.com/yihui/knitr/contributors) and users who reported
nearly 500 issues (https://github.com/yihui/knitr/issues), asked more
than 200 questions on StackOverflow
(http://stackoverflow.com/questions/tagged/knitr) and made hundreds of
comments in the knitr website (http://yihui.name/knitr/). If you want
to contribute or have any questions, please follow these links.

Regards,
Yihui
--
Yihui Xie <xiey...@gmail.com>

2215 Snedecor Hall, Ames, IA

messages.subject: Re: [knitr] knit to HTML loses traceback context
messages.subject_clean: [knitr] knit to HTML loses traceback context
messages.body_plain:
Hi Mike,

This is a very good question, and you are right that knitr is unable
to keep track of the call stacks. The reason is that the code is
evaluated within try(withCallingHandlers()) by default which will not
really signal an error.

> f = function() 1+'a'
> try(f())
Error in 1 + "a" : non-numeric argument to binary operator
> traceback()
No traceback available

You can opts_knit$set(stop_on_error = 2) and compile the document,
which will signal the real error, but that will halt the compilation.

knitr is not suitable for such tasks, especially when interaction is
needed, e.g. debug() and browser(). Note in particular that Roger's
title was "Interactive Debugging", and knitr is typically run in a
non-interactive (batch) R session.

Regards,
Yihui
--
Yihui Xie <xiey...@gmail.com>
Phone: 515-294-2465 Web: http://yihui.name
Department of Statistics, Iowa State University
2215 Snedecor Hall, Ames, IA

> Greetings. I'm trying to write up a simple introduction to the "classical"
> debugging tools in R, and I'm trying to do this in a "literate" way, using R
> Markdown.
>
> I'm basically just excerpting stuff from a document written by Roger Peng at
> Johns Hopkins:
>
> http://www.biostat.jhsph.edu/~rpeng/docs/R-debug-tools.pdf
>
> (I've asked Roger for his permission. I've taken the optimistic approach and
> assumed he'll grant it.)
>
> The first tool he discusses is "traceback", and the very simplest example of
> that is the case in which there's really only one call to begin with. For
> instance:
>
>> message(log(-1))
> Error in if (x > 0) print("Hello") else print("Goodbye") :
> missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed
> In addition: Warning message:
> In log(-1) : NaNs produced
>>
>> traceback()
> 1: message(log(-1))
>>
>
> If I put this in a code block in an R Markdown file:
>

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the discussion, everyone. Finally I decided to use the term
"Dynamic Documents" in the title. This may sound confusing to people
who are not familiar with the work of Duncan Temple Lang and Robert
Gentleman, and I will clarify this inside the book. Perhaps we should
add one more section "In computing" to the Wikipedia entry
http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Living_document

I do not want to use "Reproducible Research" in the title due to two
reasons: one is that this topic is too general for this very focused
technical book (I have one chapter on this topic in the book, though),
and the other is we actually have another book on this topic under
development.

Regards,
Yihui

messages.subject: knitcitations update and request for feedback?
messages.subject_clean: knitcitations update and request for feedback?
messages.body_plain:
Dear Knitr users,

As some of you know, I've written a little R package to accompany knitr and provide dynamic citations (in which bibliographic information is pulled from the web rather than some local bibtex file).  The package is particularly aimed at markdown/web based displays.  I've recently added a few features that may be of interest:

* The ability to cite by URL instead of DOI (including content that does not have a DOI)
* Link the in-line citation to the original source
* provide a mouse-over "tooltip" above the inline citation with the citation details
* provide semantic information about the reason for the citation, using David Shotton's CITO ontology  <http://dx.doi.org/10.1186/2041-1480-1-S1-S6>

Basic introduction appears in the README https://github.com/cboettig/knitcitations/ and a bit more about the semantics appears here <http://www.carlboettiger.info/2013/02/22/semantic-citations-for-the-notebook-and-knitr.html>:

If anyone is interested in this, I'd be happy to see any bug reports or feature requests in the issues tracker.

Thanks!

Carl

--
Carl Boettiger
UC Santa Cruz
http://www.carlboettiger.info/

messages.subject: Selectively tangle code chunks?
messages.subject_clean: Selectively tangle code chunks?
messages.body_plain:
Greetings.  I wonder if there's a way to knit/tangle only selected code chunks from an Rmd file.  This is vaguely analogous to EVALuating only selected R commands within a given code block.  I might want to collect just my function definitions in a file, for instance.  Or I might want to tangle just code chunks with chunk names that begin with 'a' (or whatever).  I understand that it isn't difficult to tangle the whole file, then use an editor (vim, emacs) to chop out the pieces I don't want, but it would be nice not to have to make the extra step.  Thanks.

-- Mike

can post-process the R script as you said, e.g. if you want all chunks
with labels a.*, you can do grep('^## @knitr a') and filter out the
code you want.
